question:
Suppose \(n^\ast\) means \(\dfrac1n,\) the reciprocal of \(n.\) For example, \(5^\ast = \dfrac15.\) How many of the following four statements are true?

\[\mathrm{(i)}\quad 3^\ast + 6^\ast = 9^\ast\]

\[\mathrm{(ii)}\quad 6^\ast - 4^\ast = 2^\ast\]

\[\mathrm{(iii)}\quad 2^\ast \cdot 6^\ast = 12^\ast\]

\[\mathrm{(iv)}\quad 10^\ast \div 2^\ast = 5^\ast\]
solution:
Replace each \(n^\ast\) by \(1/n\), then check the four equalities using ordinary fraction operations. Every starred input is nonzero, so all the reciprocals are defined.

For (i), use a common denominator:
\[
\frac13+\frac16=\frac26+\frac16=\frac12\ne\frac19.
\]
Thus (i) is false.

For (ii), use twelfths:
\[
\frac16-\frac14=\frac2{12}-\frac3{12}=-\frac1{12}\ne\frac12.
\]
Thus (ii) is false.

For (iii), multiply numerators and denominators:
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac16=\frac1{12}=12^\ast.
\]
Thus (iii) is true.

For (iv), the divisor \(2^\ast=1/2\) is nonzero. Dividing by it means multiplying by its reciprocal:
\[
\frac1{10}\div\frac12=\frac1{10}\cdot2=\frac15=5^\ast.
\]
Thus (iv) is true. Exactly \(2\) statements are true, choice C.

edges.reason: The reciprocal is characterized by a product equal to one; negative rational reciprocals use the sign of that product.
The criterion explicitly asks for the least common multiple of the denominators. An arbitrary product denominator would not meet that extra criterion.
Once denominators agree, the target adds or subtracts numerators in equal fractional units, directly using same-denominator arithmetic.
The target explicitly first rewrites unlike denominators to a common denominator. That renaming step is a required procedure here, regardless of other possible fraction-addition representations.

The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.

The integer-divisor case provides familiar reciprocal-rule practice. A general fraction-divisor rule can instead be derived directly by equalizing units or solving the defining multiplication relation; Gemini's customary first-lesson order does not make that earlier special-case procedure a necessary step.
edges.scope: extending the reciprocal rule to fractional divisors
